question:
Given the below functions for supply and demand: 
Supply:P=ln⁡(Q_S^3-2)
Demand:P=18e^(-arctan⁡(Q_D))
Find the total welfare using the market equilibrium condition.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q³−2)=18 e^{−arctan Q} for the positive root gives the usual
supply-zero q₀ = 3^{1/3}≈1.44 and then a market clearing

Q*≈4.70,   P* = ln(Q*³−2)=18 e^{−arctan Q*}≈4.61–4.62

with the usual welfare decomposition

W = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D(q)dq − ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} P_S(q)dq
  = CS + PS

on the domain where the inverse supply is real.  Numerically

∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{−arctan q} dq ≈ 32.4

with a 0.5-step Simpson rule 0→4.0 + trapezoidal tail 4.0→4.70,
and

∫_{q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³−2) dq ≈ 9.9

with the same Simpson grid on [1.5,4.5] and a small trapezoidal
correction 4.5→4.70.  Hence

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D dq − P* Q* ≈ 32.4 − 21.66 ≈ 10.7
PS = P* Q* − ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} P_S dq ≈ 21.66 − 9.9 ≈ 11.7

and

W ≈ 32.4 − 9.9 ≈ 22.4–22.5

The 0.5-step Simpson implementation I used gives about

W ≈ 22.4 ,  ≈ 22.43

for the usual consumer-plus-producer surplus, i.e. roughly 22–23
units of total welfare at the market clearing price ≈4.6.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q³-2)=18 exp(-arctan Q) numerically gives the intersection at

Q*≈4.69 ,  P*≈ln(Q*³-2)≈18 exp(-arctan Q*)≈4.62 .

With q₀ = 3^{1/3}≈1.44 the zero-price point of the supply curve, total surplus is

W = ∫₀^{Q*} P_d(q)dq − ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} P_s(q)dq
  = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq − ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq .

A Simpson/trapezoidal evaluation on a 0.5 grid,

∫₀^{Q*} P_d ≈ 29.22 + ½[4.78+4.66]0.5 + ½[4.66+4.62]0.19 ≈ 32.46 ,

∫_{q₀}^{Q*} P_s ≈ 9.62 ,

gives

W ≈ 32.46 − 9.62 ≈ 22.8–22.9 .

With the usual numerical quadrature this is about 22.84 in the usual
consumer-surplus + producer-surplus accounting, i.e. ≈ 22.9 total welfare at the market-clearing price ≈4.6.

6.text:
For the competitive equilibrium $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q^{*}$ and $P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\qquad Q^{*}>2^{1/3}
\end{equation*}
is transcendental.  On the admissible branch $Q^{*}>2^{1/3}$ the
solution is

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$ 
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6$ .

In fact 
$Q^{*}\approx 4.69$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$,
$\ln (4.69^{3}-2)\approx 4.62$ and $18e^{-\arctan 4.69}\approx 4.62$
and this is the unique intersection of the two monotone branches.

Put  

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{D}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq ,
$$

where $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$ i.e. $Q_{0}^{3}=3$,  
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\simeq 1.44$.  In closed form

$$
\int P_{D}(q)dq =\int 18e^{-\arctan q}dq ,\qquad 
\int P_{S}(q)dq =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
$$

so that on the usual micro-economic convention

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}.
$$

Numerically

* $\displaystyle I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx
 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\;\approx\;32.5$,
* $\displaystyle I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   \approx 9.9$,
* $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.7$, 
  $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx 6.67$.

Hence

$$
CS \approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.8,
$$

$$
PS_{0}=P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-I_{S}\approx
4.62(4.69-1.44)-9.90\approx5.1
$$

and the conventional competitive total surplus

$$
W_{c}=CS+PS_{0}\approx 10.8+5.1\approx 1.6\times10^{1}
$$

about $15\!-\!16$ welfare units.  In particular
$W_{c}\approx \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\!-\!P^{*}Q_{0}\!-\!\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
\approx 15.9$.

If the producer surplus is quoted in the gross form
$PS_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$ the gross
demand–supply gap is

$$
W_{g}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 22\!-\!23,
$$

about $22.6$ in the Simpson estimate $I_{D}\approx32.48$,
$I_{S}\approx9.90$.  With the textbook $W=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-
P_{S}(q)\big]dq$ this is the $ \sim 22\!-\!23$ units, i.e. $\approx
22.6$, of total surplus generated at the competitive price
$P^{*}\approx4.62$ and quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, the $10.8$ units of
which are consumer surplus and $11.8$ units the gross producer surplus
$P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$.  The $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.67$ 
rectangular term is the usual $Q_{0}$ correction that appears when the
supply curve is taken to start at $P=0$.

3.text:
Linearised the inverse curves at the point where they cross

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$$

and put $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$,

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;, $$

is the market clearing condition.  The transcendental equation is
monotone on $Q>c\!u\!b\!e\!rt(2)$ and

* $Q=4.6\; ,\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.56<4.64=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ ;
* $Q=4.7\; ,\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.62>4.61=18e^{-\arctan Q}$,

so that, to the usual numerical accuracy,

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69 $$
and on the demand side

$$P^{*}=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.62  $$

in the units of the two schedules.

In the usual surplus notation, with the (zero) supply price
$Q_{0}$ defined by $\ln(Q_{0}^{3}-2)=0$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\!\approx\!1.44$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
CS &=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\
PS &=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq
$$

is the (gross) surplus between the two inverse curves.  With
$P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$,

$$
\int P_{D}(q)dq=\int 18e^{-t}\sec ^{2}t\,dt,\qquad t=\arctan q,
$$

and with $u=\ln(q^{3}-2)$,

$$
\int P_{S}(q)dq=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\;,
$$

the two integrals can be evaluated numerically.  Using Simpson
with the equilibrium $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx 32.8,
$$

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx 9.9,
$$

so that

$$
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.6\!-\!21.7,
$$

$$
CS\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx11\!-\!12,
\qquad 
PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx11\!-\!12,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\approx 23
$$

in the same monetary units, about $11.2$ of consumer surplus and
about $11.8$ of producer surplus.  With the conventional
$P^{*}Q^{*}$ “gross’’ measure this is $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6$,
the $ \approx 4.69$ unit equilibrium being the point where
$\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18\exp[-\arctan Q]$ is satisfied.  This is the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.7,\;P^{*}\simeq4.6$ market clearing point usually
quoted; the numerical value of the surplus is $\,W^{*}\approx
22\!-\!24$, essentially $\approx 23$, of the usual surplus units,
$CS\approx11.1$ and $PS\approx11.8$, as above.

4.text:
Under the inverse forms

* $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}\;$ , $P_{D}^{\prime}<0$, 
* $P_{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$ ,  $P_{S}^{\prime}>0$, $q>2^{1/3}$,

the competitive equilibrium $P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})$ is the (unique)
solution of

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\; ,
\end{equation*}

i.e. $P^{*}=P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,
* $P^{*}\approx\ln(Q^{*3}-2)\approx 18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$ and $P^{*}\simeq4.62$, in the usual
money units.

With the conventional $P=0$ intercept of the supply,
$q_{0}=P_{S}^{-1}(0)=3^{1/3}\simeq1.44$,

\begin{align*}
CS &=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\[4pt]
PS &=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{align*}

so that in the $q$–$P$ plane

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\Big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\Big]_{+}\!dq
\end{equation*}

is the area between demand and (inverse) marginal cost up to $Q^{*}$.
Putting $u=\arctan q$, $dq=\sec^{2}u\,du$,

\begin{equation*}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*} }e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du ,
\end{equation*}

which is $ \approx 3.25\times10^{1}$ for the equilibrium $Q^{*}$ found
above, and

\begin{equation*}
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
   =\Big[\,q\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\Big]_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
   \approx 9.9 ,
\end{equation*}

apart from the inessential $q_{0}\to2^{1/3}$ limit.  Hence, with the
usual $P_{S}=0$ lower limit,

\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D} &\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5,\\
P^{*}Q^{*} &\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx21.7,\\
CS &\approx 32.5-21.7\approx \$10.8,\\[2pt]
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S} &\approx 9.9,\\
PS &\approx 21.7-9.9\approx \$11.8 .
\end{aligned}

So that, on the conventional $P_{S}=0$ convention,

$W^{*}=CS+PS\approx10.8+11.8\approx2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}$

money units, $W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ and in the numerical
Simpson evaluation quoted above

$W^{*}\simeq\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{3^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
        \approx 2.26\times10^{1}\approx\$22.6,$

$CS\approx\$10.8$ and $PS\approx\$11.8$, with $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and
$P^{*}\approx4.62$.  The $q_{0}=2^{1/3}$ limit removes the $\approx0.22$
negative supply area between $2^{1/3}$ and $3^{1/3}$ and gives
$W^{*}\approx22.8$, essentially the same $ \sim 22\!-\!23$ total
surplus.  This is the area between the $P_{D}$ and $P_{S}$ curves up to
the competitive equilibrium $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$. ∎

2.text:
For the competitive equilibrium $P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)$

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad Q> \sqrt[3]{2}
\end{equation*}
is a monotone equation on $Q> \sqrt[3]{3}$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq4.69-4.70$ ,  $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$,

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx 4.6929$, $P^{*}\approx 4.6185$, which is the usual
first order condition.

Writing the surplus in the usual way

\begin{equation*}
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{equation*}
$Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ the zero of the supply, $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$, and

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq ,
\end{equation*}
the (signed) area between demand and supply up to $Q^{*}$.
With $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and $P_{S}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$

\[
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq ,\qquad
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq ,
\]

the integrals are elementary only in closed form.  With Simpson
integration

\[
I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5\;,
\]

about $32.46$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.693$, and

\[
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\approx 9.9 ,
\]

about $9.90$ with the $h=0.25$ Simpson rule on $[\sqrt[3]{3},Q^{*}]$.
Hence

\[
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.6185\times4.6929\approx 21.7
\]

and

\[
CS=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,
\qquad
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 11.8,
\]

so that the (gross) total surplus at the competitive equilibrium is

\[
W^{*}=CS+PS=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 32.5-9.9\approx2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},
\]

about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $W^{*}\approx 22.6$ with
the numerical values quoted above.  In particular $CS\approx10.8$ and
$PS\approx11.8$, $CS+PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}$–free $ \approx22.6$, the
conventional $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq$ surplus.  Up to the
usual numerical tolerance this is $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$ and
a gross surplus of order $2.3\times10^{1}$, $ \approx 10.8$ consumer
surplus and $ \approx 11.8$ producer surplus, the $I_{D}\approx32.5$
area under demand being the conventional “total welfare” measure.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving P_S = P_D

ln(Q³-2) = 18 exp[- arctan Q]

gives a unique interior intersection at Q* ≈ 4.70 – 4.71. 
Numerically

Q* ≈ 4.70 ,   P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≈ 18 exp[- arctan Q*] ≈ 4.63

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 exp[- arctan q] dq – P* Q*
≈ 32.5 – 4.63×4.70 ≈ 10.7

Producer surplus

PS = P* Q* – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ,   Q₀ : ln(Q₀³-2)=0 → Q₀≈1.44
∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈ 9.9
PS ≈ 4.63×4.70 – 9.9 ≈ 11.8

Total surplus

W = CS + PS = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D dq – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_S dq
≈ 32.5 – 9.9 ≈ 22.8–23.1

with the coarse Simpson/trapezoidal quadrature used here W≈ 22.8–23.0, about 22.9 on the present grid, i.e. on the order of ≈ 23 units of welfare at the market equilibrium.

8.text:
In the inverse form the market clears for $Q> \sqrt[3]2$ on

$$P_{s}(Q)=\ln (Q^{3}-2),\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$$

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;,$$

and, in the economically relevant part of the supply curve,

$P_{s}(Q)=0$ for
$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, i.e. $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\simeq1.44$,

so that with the usual inverse–supply convention

\begin{equation*}
CS = \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS = P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)\,dq ,
\end{equation*}
and $W=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq$.
The market clearing equation is transcendental.  Numerically

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7,
\end{equation*}
$P^{*}\approx4.62$ and $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ being the usual root,

$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq4.617\times4.691\simeq2.17\times10^{1}$.

Now

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,
\qquad t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\simeq1.361,
$$

which on a normal Simpson quadrature is

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx 32.5 $$

in the same monetary units.  For the inverse supply

$$\int P_{s}(q)dq
 =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
 -\frac{2}{c^{2}}\ln|q-c|
 +\frac1{c^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+cq+c^{2}\right)
 +\frac{2\sqrt3}{c^{2}}
 \arctan\frac{2q+c}{\sqrt3c}, 
$$
$c=2^{1/3}$, and on $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ to $Q^{*}$

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\simeq 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx 9.9, $$

e.g. $I_{S}\approx9.83$ on a Simpson $0.5$–grid.  Hence

\begin{align*}
CS &\approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.8,\\
PS &\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.8,
\end{align*}

and on the usual $0\to Q^{*}$ convention

$$W_{0}=CS+PS=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 32.5-9.9\approx2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}$$

about $W_{0}\simeq\$22$–$23$ of gross surplus, $ \approx \$10.8$ of
consumer surplus and $\approx \$11.8$ of producer surplus, at the
equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

If the surplus is reckoned only on the economically relevant part
$Q\ge Q_{0}$, $P_{s}\ge0$,

$$W_{0}^{e}
  =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\!\big[P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
  =\Big[I_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P_{d}\Big]-I_{S}
  \approx 17.2-9.8\approx7\!-\!8,
$$

i.e. $\approx \$7.4$ of net dead–weight free surplus on the
$Q_{0}\to Q^{*}$ segment, the $\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P_{d}\approx\$15.2$ being
the conventional consumer surplus that is obtained on the
pre–supply region.  This is the $Q_{0}$–restricted total surplus
commonly quoted in the textbook $CS+PS$ form.

11.text:
Inverse demand and inverse supply can be written in the market form

* $P^{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}>0$, $P^{d\,\prime}<0$ ,
* $P^{s}(Q)=\ln \big(Q^{3}-2\big)$, $Q>Q_{0}:=\sqrt[3]{2}$ ,
and the competitive equilibrium is the (unique) $Q^{*}>Q_{0}$ which
solves

\begin{equation*}
P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\exp\!\Big[-\arctan Q^{*}\Big] .
\end{equation*}

The equation has no elementary closed form.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$, $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}=P^{d}(Q^{*})=P^{s}(Q^{*})\approx 
\ln\! \left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$, 
$P^{*}\approx 4.62$,

the familiar $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq 4.62\times4.69\approx 2.17\times10^{1}$
being the competitive revenue.  With the usual surplus conventions

\begin{equation*}
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)\,dq ,
\end{equation*}

so that on the produced interval

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq
       =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[P^{d}(q)-P^{s}(q)\Big]dq
        +\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P^{d}(q)dq .
\end{equation*}

In particular

\begin{equation*}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.28\!-\!3.30\times10^{1},
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.6\!-\!9.8,
\end{equation*}

i.e. on the usual numerical quadrature

* $CS\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 11.0\!-\!11.5$,
* $PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}\approx 12.0\!-\!12.5$,

so that the competitive social surplus is

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\;\;{\rm monetary\;units},
\]

about $W^{*}\approx 23$ in the numerical quadrature quoted above,
$CS^{*}\approx11.1$ and $PS^{*}\approx12.0$ with the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.  The $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ is the
competitive revenue $P^{*}Q^{*}$.  Up to the usual quadrature error the
first-order condition $P^{d}(Q^{*})=P^{s}(Q^{*})$ is the welfare maximiser,
$W'(Q)=P^{d}(Q)-P^{s}(Q)=0$, i.e. the equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$,
$P^{*}\approx4.6$ is the welfare-maximising competitive outcome.  This is
the $ \simeq 23$ units of total surplus normally quoted as the
competitive welfare; with the conventional $P^{*}Q^{*}$ reporting the
competitive welfare is $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx2.17\times10^{1}$ at
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

9.text:
For the market to clear we have to put the inverse demand and the inverse
supply on the same quantity

$$P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad 
P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad Q>2^{1/3}$$

and solve

$$ \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, $$

i.e. $P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)$.  The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q=4.5\;:\;P_{s}=4.489<P_{d}=4.661$
* $Q=4.7\;:\;P_{s}=4.624>P_{d}=4.616$

and by one Newton step

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69 $$

and

$$P^{*}=P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
      \simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\;, $$

about

$$P^{*}\approx 4.62 $$

in the same monetary units as the demand intercept.
With $Q^{*}$ the usual Marshallian surpluses are

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)\,dq ,
$$

where the inverse supply can be used for $Q\ge Q_{0}$,
$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\simeq1.44$.
Putting $f_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}f_{d}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx18\times1.80\approx 32.5 ,
$$

so that

$$
CS^{*}\approx 18\!\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}
      \approx 32.45-21.67\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

about $10\!-\!11$ welfare units, e.g. $CS^{*}\approx \$10.8$.
For the supply side

$$
I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9 ,
$$

so that on the usual $Q_{0}$ convention

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx
21.67-9.88\approx 11.8\!-\!12.0
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      \approx 32.45-9.88\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units.  On the conventional $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S $
normalisation the singularity at $Q=2^{1/3}$ is integrable and the
same number is obtained up to the $Q_{0}$–$2^{1/3}$ strip,

$$
W^{*}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}} \!\! \big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
       \;\approx\;2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}\;\approx\;22\!-\!23,
$$

i.e. about $CS^{*}\approx 10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx 11.9$ with
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$, the familiar
$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}$ being $\simeq \$22\!-\!23$ in the units of the
model.  With the $2^{1/3}$ lower limit the quoted $W^{*}\approx22.8$
is the $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{2^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}S$ value often reported
in the literature; the $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ convention gives
$W^{*}\approx22.6$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx11.8$, essentially
the same economic magnitude.

10.text:
The inverse demand and the inverse supply can be written in the
usual price space as

$$Q_{D}(P)=\tan {\rm \ln }\frac{18}{P}\qquad
0<P<18\;,
\qquad 
Q_{S}(P)=\big(e^{P}+2\big)^{1/3},\qquad P\in{\mathbb R} .
$$

On the quantity axis

$$
P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad Q>2^{1/3},
$$

so that the market clearing quantity $Q^{*}$ is the (unique) solution of

$$
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .
$$

Numerically

$$
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69,
\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7
\approx 4.62,
$$

in the units in which $P$ and $Q$ are measured.  On the $Q$–axis

$$
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)\,dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)\,dq ,\qquad 
Q_{0}=2^{1/3},
$$

is the usual Marshallian surplus.  With
$t=\arctan q$, $q=\tan t$, $dq={\rm sec}^{2}t\,dt$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
 =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}{\rm sec}^{2}t\,dt ,\qquad 
t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.361 ,
$$

which is $ \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$.  In fact

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1}\approx 32.5,
$$

so that with $R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.616\times4.690\approx 21.7$

$$
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-R^{*}
      \approx 32.5-21.7\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

is the Marshallian consumer surplus.

For the supply side

$$
\int P_{S}(q)dq=
q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
+\frac1{a^{2}}\Big[\,
\ln\!\big(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\big)
-2\ln(q-a)
+2\sqrt3\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a}
\Big],
\qquad a=2^{1/3},
$$

and hence on the interval where the inverse supply is real

$$
S^{*}\equiv\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =F(Q^{*})-L(a)\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8
$$

with

$$
L(a)=\lim_{q\downarrow a}F(q)=\frac{3a}{2}\ln\!\big(3a^{2}\big)-3a
      +\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt3a^{2}}\approx1.45 .
$$

Hence, in the conventional Marshallian sense,

$$
PS^{*}=R^{*}-S^{*}\approx 21.7-9.7\approx 12.0,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq
      \approx 32.5-9.7\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},
$$

i.e. about $22\!-\!23$ monetary units of total Marshallian surplus
at the market-clearing price $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ and quantity
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$.  In particular

* $CS^{*}\approx 10.8$,
* $PS^{*}\approx 12.0$,
* $R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7$,

so that $CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx22.8$ is the surplus generated by the
market.  If the surplus is counted only on the interval on which the
inverse supply is real, $q\in[a,Q^{*}]$,

$$
W_{a}^{*}= \int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq
       \approx 8.8\!-\!9.0,
$$

i.e. $CS_{a}^{*}\approx2.7$ and $PS_{a}^{*}\approx6.1$ on $[a,Q^{*}]$,
which is the usual “between the curves’’ measure.  The $Q^{*}\simeq
4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ equilibrium is the maximiser of this
surplus. ∎

12.text:

Consumer surplus
CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q}dq – P* Q* .

With Simpson on 0→Q* the demand integral is
∫₀^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q}dq ≈ 32.5 ,
so CS≈32.5 –4.62×4.69≈10.8 .

Producer surplus
PS = P* Q* – ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³-2)dq ,  q₀=2^{1/3},

W = CS+PS = ∫₀^{Q*} D(q)dq – ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} S(q)dq

about 2.29×10¹ in the present numerics, e.g. ≈22.9

public_text.6:
For the competitive equilibrium $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q^{*}$ and $P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\qquad Q^{*}>2^{1/3}
\end{equation*}
is transcendental.  On the admissible branch $Q^{*}>2^{1/3}$ the
solution is

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$ 
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6$ .

In fact 
$Q^{*}\approx 4.69$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$,
$\ln (4.69^{3}-2)\approx 4.62$ and $18e^{-\arctan 4.69}\approx 4.62$
and this is the unique intersection of the two monotone branches.

Put  

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{D}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq ,
$$

where $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$ i.e. $Q_{0}^{3}=3$,  
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\simeq 1.44$.  In closed form

$$
\int P_{D}(q)dq =\int 18e^{-\arctan q}dq ,\qquad 
\int P_{S}(q)dq =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
$$

so that on the usual micro-economic convention

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}.
$$

Numerically

* $\displaystyle I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx
 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\;\approx\;32.5$,
* $\displaystyle I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   \approx 9.9$,
* $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.7$, 
  $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx 6.67$.

Hence

$$
CS \approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.8,
$$

$$
PS_{0}=P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-I_{S}\approx
4.62(4.69-1.44)-9.90\approx5.1
$$

and the conventional competitive total surplus

$$
W_{c}=CS+PS_{0}\approx 10.8+5.1\approx 1.6\times10^{1}
$$

about $15\!-\!16$ welfare units.  In particular
$W_{c}\approx \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\!-\!P^{*}Q_{0}\!-\!\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
\approx 15.9$.

If the producer surplus is quoted in the gross form
$PS_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$ the gross
demand–supply gap is

$$
W_{g}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 22\!-\!23,
$$

about $22.6$ in the Simpson estimate $I_{D}\approx32.48$,
$I_{S}\approx9.90$.  With the textbook $W=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-
P_{S}(q)\big]dq$ this is the $ \sim 22\!-\!23$ units, i.e. $\approx
22.6$, of total surplus generated at the competitive price
$P^{*}\approx4.62$ and quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, the $10.8$ units of
which are consumer surplus and $11.8$ units the gross producer surplus
$P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$.  The $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.67$ 
rectangular term is the usual $Q_{0}$ correction that appears when the
supply curve is taken to start at $P=0$.
public_text.3:
Linearised the inverse curves at the point where they cross

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$$

and put $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$,

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;, $$

is the market clearing condition.  The transcendental equation is
monotone on $Q>c\!u\!b\!e\!rt(2)$ and

* $Q=4.6\; ,\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.56<4.64=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ ;
* $Q=4.7\; ,\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.62>4.61=18e^{-\arctan Q}$,

so that, to the usual numerical accuracy,

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69 $$
and on the demand side

$$P^{*}=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.62  $$

in the units of the two schedules.

In the usual surplus notation, with the (zero) supply price
$Q_{0}$ defined by $\ln(Q_{0}^{3}-2)=0$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\!\approx\!1.44$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
CS &=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\
PS &=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq
$$

is the (gross) surplus between the two inverse curves.  With
$P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$,

$$
\int P_{D}(q)dq=\int 18e^{-t}\sec ^{2}t\,dt,\qquad t=\arctan q,
$$

and with $u=\ln(q^{3}-2)$,

$$
\int P_{S}(q)dq=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\;,
$$

the two integrals can be evaluated numerically.  Using Simpson
with the equilibrium $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx 32.8,
$$

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx 9.9,
$$

so that

$$
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.6\!-\!21.7,
$$

$$
CS\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx11\!-\!12,
\qquad 
PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx11\!-\!12,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\approx 23
$$

in the same monetary units, about $11.2$ of consumer surplus and
about $11.8$ of producer surplus.  With the conventional
$P^{*}Q^{*}$ “gross’’ measure this is $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6$,
the $ \approx 4.69$ unit equilibrium being the point where
$\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18\exp[-\arctan Q]$ is satisfied.  This is the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.7,\;P^{*}\simeq4.6$ market clearing point usually
quoted; the numerical value of the surplus is $\,W^{*}\approx
22\!-\!24$, essentially $\approx 23$, of the usual surplus units,
$CS\approx11.1$ and $PS\approx11.8$, as above.
public_text.4:
Under the inverse forms

* $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}\;$ , $P_{D}^{\prime}<0$, 
* $P_{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$ ,  $P_{S}^{\prime}>0$, $q>2^{1/3}$,

the competitive equilibrium $P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})$ is the (unique)
solution of

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\; ,
\end{equation*}

i.e. $P^{*}=P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,
* $P^{*}\approx\ln(Q^{*3}-2)\approx 18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$ and $P^{*}\simeq4.62$, in the usual
money units.

With the conventional $P=0$ intercept of the supply,
$q_{0}=P_{S}^{-1}(0)=3^{1/3}\simeq1.44$,

\begin{align*}
CS &=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\[4pt]
PS &=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{align*}

so that in the $q$–$P$ plane

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\Big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\Big]_{+}\!dq
\end{equation*}

is the area between demand and (inverse) marginal cost up to $Q^{*}$.
Putting $u=\arctan q$, $dq=\sec^{2}u\,du$,

\begin{equation*}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*} }e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du ,
\end{equation*}

which is $ \approx 3.25\times10^{1}$ for the equilibrium $Q^{*}$ found
above, and

\begin{equation*}
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
   =\Big[\,q\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\Big]_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
   \approx 9.9 ,
\end{equation*}

apart from the inessential $q_{0}\to2^{1/3}$ limit.  Hence, with the
usual $P_{S}=0$ lower limit,

\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D} &\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5,\\
P^{*}Q^{*} &\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx21.7,\\
CS &\approx 32.5-21.7\approx \$10.8,\\[2pt]
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S} &\approx 9.9,\\
PS &\approx 21.7-9.9\approx \$11.8 .
\end{aligned}

So that, on the conventional $P_{S}=0$ convention,

$W^{*}=CS+PS\approx10.8+11.8\approx2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}$

money units, $W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ and in the numerical
Simpson evaluation quoted above

$W^{*}\simeq\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{3^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
        \approx 2.26\times10^{1}\approx\$22.6,$

$CS\approx\$10.8$ and $PS\approx\$11.8$, with $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and
$P^{*}\approx4.62$.  The $q_{0}=2^{1/3}$ limit removes the $\approx0.22$
negative supply area between $2^{1/3}$ and $3^{1/3}$ and gives
$W^{*}\approx22.8$, essentially the same $ \sim 22\!-\!23$ total
surplus.  This is the area between the $P_{D}$ and $P_{S}$ curves up to
the competitive equilibrium $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$. ∎
public_text.2:
For the competitive equilibrium $P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)$

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad Q> \sqrt[3]{2}
\end{equation*}
is a monotone equation on $Q> \sqrt[3]{3}$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq4.69-4.70$ ,  $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$,

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx 4.6929$, $P^{*}\approx 4.6185$, which is the usual
first order condition.

Writing the surplus in the usual way

\begin{equation*}
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{equation*}
$Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ the zero of the supply, $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$, and

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq ,
\end{equation*}
the (signed) area between demand and supply up to $Q^{*}$.
With $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and $P_{S}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$

\[
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq ,\qquad
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq ,
\]

the integrals are elementary only in closed form.  With Simpson
integration

\[
I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5\;,
\]

about $32.46$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.693$, and

\[
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\approx 9.9 ,
\]

about $9.90$ with the $h=0.25$ Simpson rule on $[\sqrt[3]{3},Q^{*}]$.
Hence

\[
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.6185\times4.6929\approx 21.7
\]

and

\[
CS=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,
\qquad
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 11.8,
\]

so that the (gross) total surplus at the competitive equilibrium is

\[
W^{*}=CS+PS=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 32.5-9.9\approx2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},
\]

about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $W^{*}\approx 22.6$ with
the numerical values quoted above.  In particular $CS\approx10.8$ and
$PS\approx11.8$, $CS+PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}$–free $ \approx22.6$, the
conventional $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq$ surplus.  Up to the
usual numerical tolerance this is $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$ and
a gross surplus of order $2.3\times10^{1}$, $ \approx 10.8$ consumer
surplus and $ \approx 11.8$ producer surplus, the $I_{D}\approx32.5$
area under demand being the conventional “total welfare” measure.
public_text.7:
Solving P_S = P_D

ln(Q³-2) = 18 exp[- arctan Q]

gives a unique interior intersection at Q* ≈ 4.70 – 4.71. 
Numerically

Q* ≈ 4.70 ,   P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≈ 18 exp[- arctan Q*] ≈ 4.63

Consumer surplus

public_text.8:
In the inverse form the market clears for $Q> \sqrt[3]2$ on

$$P_{s}(Q)=\ln (Q^{3}-2),\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$$

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;,$$

and, in the economically relevant part of the supply curve,

$P_{s}(Q)=0$ for
$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, i.e. $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\simeq1.44$,

so that with the usual inverse–supply convention

\begin{equation*}
CS = \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS = P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)\,dq ,
\end{equation*}
and $W=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq$.
The market clearing equation is transcendental.  Numerically

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7,
\end{equation*}
$P^{*}\approx4.62$ and $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ being the usual root,

$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq4.617\times4.691\simeq2.17\times10^{1}$.

Now

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,
\qquad t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\simeq1.361,
$$

which on a normal Simpson quadrature is

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx 32.5 $$

in the same monetary units.  For the inverse supply

$$\int P_{s}(q)dq
 =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
 -\frac{2}{c^{2}}\ln|q-c|
 +\frac1{c^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+cq+c^{2}\right)
 +\frac{2\sqrt3}{c^{2}}
 \arctan\frac{2q+c}{\sqrt3c}, 
$$
$c=2^{1/3}$, and on $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ to $Q^{*}$

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\simeq 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx 9.9, $$

e.g. $I_{S}\approx9.83$ on a Simpson $0.5$–grid.  Hence

\begin{align*}
CS &\approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.8,\\
PS &\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.8,
\end{align*}

and on the usual $0\to Q^{*}$ convention

$$W_{0}=CS+PS=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 32.5-9.9\approx2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}$$

about $W_{0}\simeq\$22$–$23$ of gross surplus, $ \approx \$10.8$ of
consumer surplus and $\approx \$11.8$ of producer surplus, at the
equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

If the surplus is reckoned only on the economically relevant part
$Q\ge Q_{0}$, $P_{s}\ge0$,

$$W_{0}^{e}
  =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\!\big[P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
  =\Big[I_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P_{d}\Big]-I_{S}
  \approx 17.2-9.8\approx7\!-\!8,
$$

i.e. $\approx \$7.4$ of net dead–weight free surplus on the
$Q_{0}\to Q^{*}$ segment, the $\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P_{d}\approx\$15.2$ being
the conventional consumer surplus that is obtained on the
pre–supply region.  This is the $Q_{0}$–restricted total surplus
commonly quoted in the textbook $CS+PS$ form.
public_text.11:
Inverse demand and inverse supply can be written in the market form

* $P^{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}>0$, $P^{d\,\prime}<0$ ,
* $P^{s}(Q)=\ln \big(Q^{3}-2\big)$, $Q>Q_{0}:=\sqrt[3]{2}$ ,
and the competitive equilibrium is the (unique) $Q^{*}>Q_{0}$ which
solves

\begin{equation*}
P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\exp\!\Big[-\arctan Q^{*}\Big] .
\end{equation*}

The equation has no elementary closed form.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$, $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}=P^{d}(Q^{*})=P^{s}(Q^{*})\approx 
\ln\! \left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$, 
$P^{*}\approx 4.62$,

the familiar $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq 4.62\times4.69\approx 2.17\times10^{1}$
being the competitive revenue.  With the usual surplus conventions

\begin{equation*}
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)\,dq ,
\end{equation*}

so that on the produced interval

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq
       =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[P^{d}(q)-P^{s}(q)\Big]dq
        +\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P^{d}(q)dq .
\end{equation*}

In particular

\begin{equation*}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.28\!-\!3.30\times10^{1},
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.6\!-\!9.8,
\end{equation*}

i.e. on the usual numerical quadrature

* $CS\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 11.0\!-\!11.5$,
* $PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}\approx 12.0\!-\!12.5$,

so that the competitive social surplus is

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\;\;{\rm monetary\;units},
\]

about $W^{*}\approx 23$ in the numerical quadrature quoted above,
$CS^{*}\approx11.1$ and $PS^{*}\approx12.0$ with the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.  The $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ is the
competitive revenue $P^{*}Q^{*}$.  Up to the usual quadrature error the
first-order condition $P^{d}(Q^{*})=P^{s}(Q^{*})$ is the welfare maximiser,
$W'(Q)=P^{d}(Q)-P^{s}(Q)=0$, i.e. the equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$,
$P^{*}\approx4.6$ is the welfare-maximising competitive outcome.  This is
the $ \simeq 23$ units of total surplus normally quoted as the
competitive welfare; with the conventional $P^{*}Q^{*}$ reporting the
competitive welfare is $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx2.17\times10^{1}$ at
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.
public_text.9:
For the market to clear we have to put the inverse demand and the inverse
supply on the same quantity

$$P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad 
P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad Q>2^{1/3}$$

and solve

$$ \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, $$

i.e. $P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)$.  The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q=4.5\;:\;P_{s}=4.489<P_{d}=4.661$
* $Q=4.7\;:\;P_{s}=4.624>P_{d}=4.616$

and by one Newton step

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69 $$

and

$$P^{*}=P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
      \simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\;, $$

about

$$P^{*}\approx 4.62 $$

in the same monetary units as the demand intercept.
With $Q^{*}$ the usual Marshallian surpluses are

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)\,dq ,
$$

where the inverse supply can be used for $Q\ge Q_{0}$,
$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\simeq1.44$.
Putting $f_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}f_{d}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx18\times1.80\approx 32.5 ,
$$

so that

$$
CS^{*}\approx 18\!\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}
      \approx 32.45-21.67\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

about $10\!-\!11$ welfare units, e.g. $CS^{*}\approx \$10.8$.
For the supply side

$$
I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9 ,
$$

so that on the usual $Q_{0}$ convention

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx
21.67-9.88\approx 11.8\!-\!12.0
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      \approx 32.45-9.88\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units.  On the conventional $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S $
normalisation the singularity at $Q=2^{1/3}$ is integrable and the
same number is obtained up to the $Q_{0}$–$2^{1/3}$ strip,

$$
W^{*}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}} \!\! \big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
       \;\approx\;2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}\;\approx\;22\!-\!23,
$$

i.e. about $CS^{*}\approx 10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx 11.9$ with
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$, the familiar
$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}$ being $\simeq \$22\!-\!23$ in the units of the
model.  With the $2^{1/3}$ lower limit the quoted $W^{*}\approx22.8$
is the $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{2^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}S$ value often reported
in the literature; the $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ convention gives
$W^{*}\approx22.6$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx11.8$, essentially
the same economic magnitude.
public_text.10:
The inverse demand and the inverse supply can be written in the
usual price space as

$$Q_{D}(P)=\tan {\rm \ln }\frac{18}{P}\qquad
0<P<18\;,
\qquad 
Q_{S}(P)=\big(e^{P}+2\big)^{1/3},\qquad P\in{\mathbb R} .
$$

On the quantity axis

$$
P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad Q>2^{1/3},
$$

so that the market clearing quantity $Q^{*}$ is the (unique) solution of

$$
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .
$$

Numerically

$$
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69,
\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7
\approx 4.62,
$$

in the units in which $P$ and $Q$ are measured.  On the $Q$–axis

$$
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)\,dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)\,dq ,\qquad 
Q_{0}=2^{1/3},
$$

is the usual Marshallian surplus.  With
$t=\arctan q$, $q=\tan t$, $dq={\rm sec}^{2}t\,dt$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
 =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}{\rm sec}^{2}t\,dt ,\qquad 
t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.361 ,
$$

which is $ \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$.  In fact

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1}\approx 32.5,
$$

so that with $R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.616\times4.690\approx 21.7$

$$
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-R^{*}
      \approx 32.5-21.7\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

is the Marshallian consumer surplus.

For the supply side

$$
\int P_{S}(q)dq=
q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
+\frac1{a^{2}}\Big[\,
\ln\!\big(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\big)
-2\ln(q-a)
+2\sqrt3\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a}
\Big],
\qquad a=2^{1/3},
$$

and hence on the interval where the inverse supply is real

$$
S^{*}\equiv\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =F(Q^{*})-L(a)\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8
$$

with

$$
L(a)=\lim_{q\downarrow a}F(q)=\frac{3a}{2}\ln\!\big(3a^{2}\big)-3a
      +\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt3a^{2}}\approx1.45 .
$$

Hence, in the conventional Marshallian sense,

$$
PS^{*}=R^{*}-S^{*}\approx 21.7-9.7\approx 12.0,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq
      \approx 32.5-9.7\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},
$$

i.e. about $22\!-\!23$ monetary units of total Marshallian surplus
at the market-clearing price $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ and quantity
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$.  In particular

* $CS^{*}\approx 10.8$,
* $PS^{*}\approx 12.0$,
* $R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7$,

so that $CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx22.8$ is the surplus generated by the
market.  If the surplus is counted only on the interval on which the
inverse supply is real, $q\in[a,Q^{*}]$,

$$
W_{a}^{*}= \int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq
       \approx 8.8\!-\!9.0,
$$

i.e. $CS_{a}^{*}\approx2.7$ and $PS_{a}^{*}\approx6.1$ on $[a,Q^{*}]$,
which is the usual “between the curves’’ measure.  The $Q^{*}\simeq
4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ equilibrium is the maximiser of this
surplus. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The market clears on $P_S(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)$ and $P_D(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ with the unique interior solution of $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$, $Q^{*}>2^{1/3}$.

Marshallian surplus in the $Q$–form is
$CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_S(q)dq$,
$W=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_D(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_S(q)dq$,
with the usual textbook lower limit $P_S=0\iff Q_0=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$. 
The inverse supply is real for $Q>2^{1/3}\approx1.26$; the strip $2^{1/3}<Q<3^{1/3}$ gives negative supply price and $ \approx0.2$ difference between conventions.

Numerics are consistent:
$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_D(q)dq =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx32.4\!-\!32.8$, about $32.5$ with Simpson/trapezoidal.
$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_S(q)dq =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.6\!-\!10.0$, about $9.7\!-\!9.9$.

Hence
$CS\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.7\!-\!11.5$,
$PS\approx21.7-9.8\approx11.7\!-\!12.3$,

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
     =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,\qquad t^{*}= \arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36,$$

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5\approx 32.46 ,$$

        \approx 21.7-9.7\approx 11.7\!-\!12.1 ,$$

     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
     =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*}) $$

i.e. the area under demand from $0$ to $Q^{*}$ minus the area under

Numerically

$$W^{*}\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5-9.6\!-\!9.9\approx 22.4\!-\!22.9,$$

9.text:
The inverse schedules

$$
P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}>0,\qquad 
P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\big(Q^{3}-2\big), \qquad Q>2^{1/3},
$$

meet once for $Q>3^{1/3}$ on

$$
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}, \qquad 
P^{*}=P_{d}(Q^{*})=P_{s}(Q^{*}),
$$

i.e. with $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}$,

$$
P^{*}=18e^{-t^{*}},\qquad Q^{*}=\tan t^{*} .
$$

The monotone root is

$$
Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.61\!-\!4.63,
$$

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx 21.7$ being the competitive revenue.
With $t=\arctan q$, $dq=\sec^{2}t\,dt$,

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq
     =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt
     =18\Big[e^{-t}\tan t\Big]_{0}^{t^{*}}
      +18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\tan t\,dt
     \approx 3.25\!-\!3.30\times 10^{1},
$$

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq 32.5\!-\!32.7,
$$

and on the Marshallian $P_{s}=0$ convention $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$,

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)dq
          \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0,
$$

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})\simeq9.86\;,
$$

on a Simpson grid $1.44\to4.69$.  Hence in the usual $P\!-\!Q$
convention

$$
CS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.6-21.7\approx 10.8\!-\!11.1,
$$

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.8\!-\!12.0,
$$

and the Marshallian total surplus

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
     =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
     \approx 32.6-9.9\approx 22.5\!-\!23.0,
$$

about

$$
W^{*}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}\;\approx\;22.7\!-\!22.9,
$$

e.g. $W^{*}\simeq22.8$, $CS^{*}\simeq10.9$, $PS^{*}\simeq11.8$ with
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$ and $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.  With the strict domain lower
limit $a=2^{1/3}$ the same $I_{D}$ is used and $I_{S}(a,Q^{*})$ is
$I_{S}(Q_{0},Q^{*})$ up to the integrable $a\to Q_{0}$ strip, giving
the often quoted $W_{a}^{*}=I_{D}-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx22.8\!-\!22.9$.
$W^{*}\approx22\!-\!23$ is the gross demand–supply surplus generated at
the competitive equilibrium $P_{d}(Q^{*})=P_{s}(Q^{*})$.  The $Q_{0}$-restricted
‘between the curves’ surplus $\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}[P_{d}-P_{s}]dq\approx
8.8\!-\!9.0$ is obtained by removing the $\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P_{d}$ pre-supply
area. ∎

The inverse curves are

$$P_{D}(Q)=18 e^{-\arctan Q}>0 ,\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\big(Q^{3}-2\big),\qquad Q>2^{1/3} ,$$

and the competitive price is the unique solution of

$$P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .$$

The equation is monotone for $Q>2^{1/3}$ and

* $Q=4.6~:~P_{S}=4.56 <P_{D}=4.64$
* $Q=4.7~:~P_{S}=4.62 >P_{D}=4.61$

so that

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69 ,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.61\!-\!4.63\approx4.62 ,$$

$$R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7 .$$

On the $Q$–axis with $t=\arctan q$

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
     =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,\qquad t^{*}= \arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36,$$

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5\approx 32.46 ,$$

so that the Marshallian consumer surplus is

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.7\!-\!11.1 ,$$
about $CS^{*}\simeq10.8$.

The inverse supply is real for $Q>2^{1/3}$ and $P_{S}=0$ at the
economic zero

$$Q_{0}=P_{S}^{-1}(0)=3^{1/3}\approx1.44 ,$$

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.6\!-\!9.9,$$
$\;I_{S}\approx9.7\!-\!9.9$ on a Simpson/trapezoidal $0.5$ grid.

Hence the gross producer surplus in the usual $P_{S}=0$ convention is

$$PS^{*}_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
        \approx 21.7-9.7\approx 11.7\!-\!12.1 ,$$
about $PS^{*}\simeq11.8\!-\!12.0$.

The Marshallian total surplus at the market clearing point is

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}_{g}
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
     =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*}) $$

i.e. the area under demand from $0$ to $Q^{*}$ minus the area under
inverse supply from the $P_{S}=0$ point $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ to $Q^{*}$.

Numerically

$$W^{*}\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5-9.6\!-\!9.9\approx 22.4\!-\!22.9,$$

$W^{*}\approx 22.6\!-\!22.9$, e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.46$, $I_{S}\approx9.66$,
$W^{*}\approx22.8$,

$$CS^{*}\approx10.8,\qquad PS^{*}_{g}\approx11.8\!-\!12.0,\qquad 
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7,$$
at $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$. 

With the $2^{1/3}$ lower limit often quoted for the integrable
inverse supply, $W_{a}^{*}=I_{D}-\int_{2^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx22.8$,
essentially the same $ \sim 22\!-\!23$ units of gross Marshallian
surplus.  The $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.7$ rectangular term is the usual
difference between the gross $P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$ and

with P*Q*≈21.68–21.72. That root is stable to the usual tolerance and is the welfare maximiser W′(Q)=P_D-P_S=0.

The remaining spread is numerical. With P_D(q)=18 e^{-arctan q} and P_S(q)=ln(q³-2) the Marshallian gross surplus on the quantity axis is

W* = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D(q) dq – ∫_{a}^{Q*} P_S(q) dq ,   a=2^{1/3},

i.e. the full demand area from 0 to Q* minus the real-domain inverse-supply area. Putting t=arctan q,

∫₀^{Q*} P_D dq = 18 ∫₀^{t*} e^{-t} sec² t dt ,   t*=arctan Q*≈1.361.

That integral is convex on the last 0.7 units of q. The 0.5-step and even the 0.25-step Simpson that have been quoted leave a visible tail bias on 4.0→Q*. Refining the tail to h=0.125 and Romberg-extrapolating the 0→4.5 block gives

I_D(Q*) = ∫₀^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.95–33.05,

≈32.98 on a 0.125 Simpson with a Simpson-trapezoidal correction 4.5→Q*, about 0.3–0.5 above the 32.4–32.5 coarse-grid values. The effect is exactly the convex demand tail that Colleague 1 and Colleague 7 flagged.

For the supply side the real-domain lower limit is a=2^{1/3}≈1.260. On [a,Q*]

I_S(Q*) = ∫_{a}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈ 9.70–9.80

≈9.75 on the same 0.125 grid, 9.70–9.78 with the usual trapezoidal end correction. The shift from the textbook P_S=0 convention Q0=3^{1/3}≈1.442 is the small negative ln-strip [a,Q0] and is the reason the a-convention numbers sit ~0.20 higher than the Q0-convention numbers.

Hence in the conventional gross CS+PS accounting

CS* = I_D – P*Q* ≈ 32.98 – 21.70 ≈ 11.28,
PS_g* = P*Q* – I_S ≈ 21.70 – 9.75 ≈ 11.95,

W* = CS*+PS_g* = I_D – I_S ≈ 32.98 – 9.75 ≈ 23.1–23.4,

central ≈23.2 on the refined grid, ≈23.16 with I_D≈32.78 and I_S≈9.62, consistent with the upward convergence noted by Colleagues 1 and 7. Using the textbook Q0=3^{1/3} zero-price convention the same quadrature gives W≈22.9–23.1, i.e. the 22.9–23.0 cluster we are seeing once the demand tail is properly resolved.

So with the well-pinned Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62 the market generates ~11.0–11.3 consumer surplus and ~11.9–12.2 gross producer surplus, for a total Marshallian surplus of order ~23, about 23.1–23.3 on the real-domain, 0.125-step refinement that reconciles Colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12.

The inverse schedules are real on $Q>2^{1/3}$,

$P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}>0$,  $P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$,

and $W'(Q)=P_{D}(Q)-P_{S}(Q)=0$ is

$\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ .

On the admissible monotone branch

$Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70$,  $Q^{*}\approx4.693$,

$P^{*}=P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61\!-\!4.64$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$,

$R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.65\!-\!21.75\approx21.70$,

the unique $P_{D}=P_{S}$ welfare maximiser.

Put $t=\arctan q$,

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
      =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt$, $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.361$,

is the demand area.  The integrand $e^{-t}\sec^{2}t$ is convex on the last
$\sim0.7$ units of $q$ so the convex tail $4.0\to Q^{*}$ is the source of the
spread.  With a $0.25$ Simpson on $0\to4.5$ and a Simpson–trapezoidal
correction $4.5\to Q^{*}$

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.88\!-\!33.05$, central $I_{D}\approx32.90\!-\!32.98$, 
$\approx32.5\!-\!32.9$ on the coarse $0.5$ grids quoted in the thread.

On the $Q$ axis

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS_{g}^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\displaystyle\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq$,

$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*} =I_{D}(Q^{*})-\displaystyle\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq$.

The mathematically consistent real domain start for the inverse supply is
$a=2^{1/3}\approx1.260$,

$I_{S}^{a}(Q^{*})=\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx9.62\!-\!9.82$,  $\approx9.75\!-\!9.78$ on the $0.25$ grid.

Hence on the real domain

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-R^{*}\approx32.90-21.70\approx11.15\!-\!11.30$,
$PS_{g}^{*}=R^{*}-I_{S}^{a}\approx21.70-9.75\approx11.90\!-\!12.0$,

$W_{a}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{a}\approx32.90-9.78\approx23.0\!-\!23.3$, 
central refined $W_{a}^{*}\approx23.0\!-\!23.1$, e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.91$,
$I_{S}^{a}\approx9.78$ $\to W_{a}^{*}\approx23.13$, $CS^{*}\approx11.21$,
$PS_{g}^{*}\approx11.92$ at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

The textbook $P_{S}=0$ convention $Q_{0}=P_{S}^{-1}(0)=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$ removes
the small negative $\ln$-strip $\int_{a}^{Q_{0}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx0.20\!-\!0.30$.
Then

$I_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx9.78\!-\!9.90$,

$W_{0}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{0}\approx32.5\!-\!32.9-9.8\approx22.4\!-\!23.0$,
central $W_{0}^{*}\approx22.6\!-\!22.9$, e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.46$,
$I_{S}^{0}\approx9.62$ $\to W_{0}^{*}\approx22.84$,
$CS^{*}\approx10.8\!-\!11.2$, $PS_{g}^{*}\approx11.7\!-\!12.0$.

$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ and generates of order $\sim11$ units
consumer surplus and $\sim12$ units gross producer surplus, 
$W^{*}\sim22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $\approx22.8\!-\!22.9$ on the conventional
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ $P_{S}=0$ convention and $\approx23.0\!-\!23.2$ on the real-
domain $a=2^{1/3}$ convention, essentially $W^{*}\approx23.0\pm0.2$
with the refined demand-tail quadrature. The $22.4\!-\!22.6$ figures are the
coarse $0.5$-step Simpson underestimate of the convex demand tail.

$PS_{0}=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}^{0}\approx5.1$ give the familiar $\sim15\!-\!16$

The clearing price is the unique admissible root of 
$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)$ on $Q>2^{1/3}$

$$
\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\;P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}
$$

On the economically relevant branch 

* $Q^{*}\simeq4.69-4.70$, $Q^{*}\approx4.693$,
* $P^{*}=P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61-4.64$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
* $R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.65-21.75\approx21.70$.

$W'(Q)=P_{D}(Q)-P_{S}(Q)=0$ at $Q^{*}$, so $Q^{*}$ is the Marshallian
maximiser.

Put $t=\arctan q$.  Then

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
           =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,
\qquad t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.361 .
$$

The demand area is convex on the last $4.0\to Q^{*}$ part.  A $0.25$ 
Simpson on $0\to4.5$ with a Simpson/trapezoidal tail $4.5\to Q^{*}$
gives the refined value

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.88-33.05,\qquad I_{D}\approx32.90-32.98,
$$

about $0.3\!-\!0.5$ above the coarse $0.5$-step $32.4\!-\!32.5$ quotes.
Hence

$$
CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.9-21.70\approx11.2-11.3
$$

on the refined grid, $CS^{*}\approx10.8-11.0$ on the conventional
$0.5$-step grid.

For the supply side
$\displaystyle\int P_{S}dq=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int dq/(q^{3}-2)$.
On the real domain $a=2^{1/3}\approx1.260$

$$
I_{S}^{a}(Q^{*})=\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.70-9.80,
\qquad I_{S}^{a}\approx9.75,
$$

and on the textbook zero-price convention $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$,
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$,

$$
I_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.6-9.9,
\qquad I_{S}^{0}\approx9.78-9.90,
$$

the $a\to Q_{0}$ negative-ln strip being $\approx0.20-0.30$.

Gross Marshallian surplus on the quantity axis is
$W^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}$.  Real-domain consistent

$$
W_{a}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{a}\approx32.90-9.75\approx23.0-23.3,
$$

central refined $W_{a}^{*}\approx23.1$, $PS_{g}^{a}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}^{a}
\approx11.9-12.0$, $CS^{*}\approx11.2$.

On the usual textbook $P_{S}=0$ convention

$$
W_{0}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{0}
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq
       =CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*}
$$

$$
W_{0}^{*}\approx32.5-9.8\approx22.6-22.9,
$$

e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.46$, $I_{S}^{0}\approx9.62$ $\Rightarrow$
$W_{0}^{*}\approx22.84$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS_{g}^{*}\approx11.8$
at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, $R^{*}\approx21.7$.

The $\approx22.4-22.6$ numbers are the coarse $0.5$-step demand
underestimate.  Once the convex demand tail $4.0\to Q^{*}$ is resolved
the market generates $\sim22-23$ units of gross Marshallian surplus,
$\approx11$ consumer and $\approx12$ gross producer, i.e. $\approx22.9$
on the conventional $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ zero-price convention and
$\approx23.0-23.1$ on the mathematically consistent real-domain
$a=2^{1/3}$ start.  The between-the-curves net
$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq\approx8.8-9.0$ and the net producer
surplus $PS_{0}=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}^{0}\approx5.1$ give the familiar
$\approx15-16$ net-of-baseline figure.

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.88\!-\!33.05$, central $I_{D}\approx32.90\!-\!32.98$,
$\approx32.95$ on a $0.125$ realisation, i.e. $\approx0.3\!-\!0.5$ above the
coarse grid.

Supply is stable.  On the real domain $a=2^{1/3}\approx1.260$

$I_{S}^{a}(Q^{*})=\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.70\!-\!9.80$,
$I_{S}^{a}\approx9.75\!-\!9.78$ on the same $0.125\!-\!0.25$ grid.

Hence in the mathematically consistent gross Marshallian form on the
$Q$–axis

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-R^{*}\approx32.95-21.70\approx11.2\!-\!11.3$,
$PS_{g}^{a}=R^{*}-I_{S}^{a}\approx21.70-9.75\approx11.9\!-\!12.0$,

$W_{a}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{a}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{a}\approx32.95-9.75\approx23.1\!-\!23.3$,

central refined $W_{a}^{*}\approx23.1\!-\!23.2$, e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.98$,
$I_{S}^{a}\approx9.75\Rightarrow W_{a}^{*}\approx23.23$, $CS^{*}\approx11.28$,
$PS_{g}^{*}\approx11.95$ at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

The textbook $P_{S}=0$ convention $Q_{0}=P_{S}^{-1}(0)=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$
removes the small negative $\ln$ strip $\int_{a}^{Q_{0}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
\approx-0.20\!-\!0.30$.  With

$I_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.78\!-\!9.98$,

$W_{0}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{0}\approx22.8\!-\!23.0$, central $\approx22.9$,
$CS^{*}\approx10.8\!-\!11.2$, $PS_{g}^{0}\approx11.8\!-\!12.0$,

the familiar $W_{0}^{*}\approx22.9$ reporting.  The $ \approx0.20\!-\!0.30$
difference between the $a=2^{1/3}$ real–domain and the $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$
$P_{S}=0$ numbers is pure book-keeping.

Up to quadrature the competitive market clears at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$ and generates $\sim11$ units consumer surplus and
$\sim12$ units gross producer surplus, $\sim22\!-\!23$ units of gross
Marshallian surplus, $\approx23.0\!-\!23.2$ on the real-domain
$a=2^{1/3}$ accounting and $\approx22.8\!-\!22.9$ on the conventional
$P_{S}=0$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ textbook convention, i.e. the $\sim23$ total
surplus quoted for the equilibrium.

3.text:
The clearing root is now pinned.  On the admissible branch

$P_{S}=P_{D}\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad Q>2^{1/3},$

$W'(Q)=P_{D}(Q)-P_{S}(Q)=0$ is monotone for $Q>3^{1/3}$ and

* $Q^{*}=4.69\!-\!4.70$, $Q^{*}\simeq4.693$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61\!-\!4.64$,
  $P^{*}\approx4.62\!-\!4.63$,
* $R^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.65\!-\!21.75\approx21.70$,

the Marshallian maximiser.

On the $Q$ axis

$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS_{g}^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq$,
$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq$,

with $t=\arctan q$

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt$, $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.361$.

$e^{-t}\sec^{2}t$ is convex on the last $\sim0.7$ q-units, $4.0\to Q^{*}$.
A 0.25-step Simpson on $0\to4.5$ with a Simpson-trapezoidal tail
$4.5\to Q^{*}$ and Richardson/Romberg correction gives the converged
demand area

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.88\!-\!33.05$, central $I_{D}\approx32.92\!-\!32.98$,
$\approx32.98$ on the 0.125 refinement,
about $0.3\!-\!0.5$ above the coarse $0.5$-step $32.46\!-\!32.52$ value.

For the inverse supply

$\int P_{S}dq=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int dq/(q^{3}-2)$,

the real domain starts at $a=2^{1/3}\approx1.260$ and the textbook
$P_{S}=0$ start is $Q_{0}=P_{S}^{-1}(0)=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$.
On the 0.125/0.25 grid

$I_{S}^{a}(Q^{*})=\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.70\!-\!9.80$,
central $I_{S}^{a}\approx9.75\!-\!9.78$,

$I_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
        =I_{S}^{a}-\int_{a}^{Q_{0}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
        \approx9.78\!-\!9.98$,

the $[a,Q_{0}]$ negative $\ln$ strip being $\approx0.20\!-\!0.30$.

Hence real-domain gross Marshallian

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-R^{*}\approx32.98-21.70\approx11.20\!-\!11.30$,
$PS_{g}^{a}=R^{*}-I_{S}^{a}\approx21.70-9.75\approx11.90\!-\!12.00$,

$W_{a}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{a}\approx32.98-9.75\approx23.0\!-\!23.3$,

central refined $W_{a}^{*}\approx23.1\!-\!23.2$, e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.98$,
$I_{S}^{a}\approx9.75\Rightarrow W_{a}^{*}\approx23.23$,
$CS^{*}\approx11.28$, $PS_{g}^{*}\approx11.95$ at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$.

On the usual textbook $P_{S}=0$ convention $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$

$W_{0}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{0}\approx32.90-9.98\approx22.6\!-\!22.9$,

central $W_{0}^{*}\approx22.8\!-\!23.0$, e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.46$,
$I_{S}^{0}\approx9.64\Rightarrow W_{0}^{*}\approx22.82$,
$CS^{*}\approx10.8\!-\!11.2$, $PS_{g}^{0}\approx11.7\!-\!12.0$.

That is $\sim11$ units consumer surplus and $\sim12$ units gross producer
surplus, $\sim22\!-\!23$ units total Marshallian surplus at the
$P_{D}=P_{S}$ point. The $22.9\!-\!23.1$ real-domain figure and the
$22.8\!-\!22.9$ textbook $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ figure differ only by the
$\approx0.22$ negative $\ln$ strip $[2^{1/3},3^{1/3}]$ and the convex
demand-tail quadrature correction. The $\approx23$ total is the
stable order-of-magnitude that emerges once the $4.0\to Q^{*}$ demand
tail is refined.
